newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - SNB sees no need to change monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - SNB sees no need to change monetary policy.

text.p: Switzerland's tentative economy recovery is not strong enough to warrant any change in the Swiss National Bank's generous monetary policy at this stage, SNB Chairman Hans Meyer said on Thursday.

"The economic recovery is not far enough along now so that an adjustment of monetary policy is urgent. There are still some risks," Meyer said at the SNB's semi-annual news conference, repeating forecasts the economy would grow 0.5 percent in 1997.
Meyer said the SNB had stated on several occasions it would only consider tightening its generous policy when there were clear signs an economic recovery was under way.
"Today there are various signs that the Swiss economy has bottomed out and is beginning to pick up slightly," he said.
Meyer noted that Swiss first-quarter gross domestic product did not decline based on the fourth quarter of 1996, although it was roughly one percent below the previous year's first quarter.
Private consumption has also revived and developments in exports were also encouraging.
But he said that problems in the domestic economy, including the construction industry, could not be ignored.
His comments confirmed financial markets' expectations that the SNB would stick to its expansive course. The Swiss franc eased against the dollar and mark, while shares opened higher.
Despite recent overshooting of the SNB's monetary base versus the target for growth of roughly one percent per year, Meyer said current policy did not pose a great threat to price stability.

"This overshooting is justified by the current economic situation," Meyer said. He also said that broader monetary aggregates were showing less signs of serious expansion and that their growth was expected to slow in coming months.
"Our monetary policy thus poses no direct inflationary threat. In spite of that, we will remain vigilant," he said.
Meyer said the timing of any future tightening of monetary policy would depend on the state of the economy and the Swiss franc's foreign exchange rates.

"When it comes to choosing the proper time there are two factors especially which must be considered: the state of the Swiss economy and development in the exchange rate, which for the foreseeable future will depend mainly on events pertaining to the plan for European monetary union," he said.
SNB officials made clear they would fight to keep the Swiss franc from rising if investors park money in the currency amid jitters that Europe's single euro currency could be weak.

SNB board member Bruno Gehrig said the current strength of the Swiss franc was unjustified and the appreciation had been caused by increased uncertainty about Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).
"We consider such an appreciation unjustified and reacted to it," Gehrig said.

Since last month, the SNB has injected extra liquidity on occasion to bring down money market rates and thus counter upwards pressure on the Swiss franc. Since then it has gradually reduced rates on its money market operations to 1.00 percent most recently, from levels around 1-5/8 percent in early May.
"We said at our last meeting with the press that we would resist any unrealistic distortion in the exchange rate and we will continue to do this," Gehrig added.
Gehrig noted that since early March the external value of the Swiss franc had risen some 3.5 percent on a trade-weighted basis, reversing the weakening trend during the last year.
"The current strength of the franc is mainly due to the events and expectations of the European economic and monetary union," Gehrig said.

Signs that the German budget deficit would grow and the controversy over the Bundesbank's gold had increased uncertainties over whether the Maastricht stability criteria could be rigorously maintained, he said, adding that the elections in France then also unsettled the markets.
"While the financial markets were confident for a long time, recent events paved the way for a more sceptical judgement," Gehrig said.
